items.title: Amoakohene formally bows out as NDC Ashanti Regional Secretary, touts party’s electoral gains
items.description: Ashanti Regional Minister Dr Frank Amoakohene has formally ended his tenure as Ashanti Regional Secretary of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), following the successful conclusion of the party’s regional executive elections. In a Facebook post announcing his departure, Dr Amoakohene described his service in the position as one of the greatest honours of his life, while reflecting on what he considers significant achievements recorded by the party in the Ashanti Region during his tenure. He said the NDC had made considerable electoral progress in the region, traditionally regarded as a stronghold of the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP), despite the challenges associated with expanding its political influence there. According to him, the party increased its parliamentary representation in the region from four seats to seven, while also narrowing the electoral gap in several other constituencies. He further disclosed that the NDC improved its presidential vote share in the Ashanti Region from approximately 26.5 per cent in the 2020 general election to more than 34 per cent in 2024. Dr Amoakohene described the gains as achievements that many had previously considered impossible, crediting the collective efforts of party members and supporters. “Together, we achieved what many said was impossible in Ashanti,” he said. Beyond the electoral gains, he highlighted the completion of the Ashanti Regional Party Secretariat as another major achievement during his tenure. He acknowledged the contributions of party members and predecessors who initiated the project, expressing gratitude for the opportunity to complete an initiative started by earlier generations of NDC leadership. “We were privileged to finish what they began,” he said. Dr Amoakohene also expressed appreciation to President John Dramani Mahama and the party’s national executives for their leadership and guidance throughout his period in office. He stressed that the achievements could not be attributed to one individual, acknowledging the contributions of constituency executives, branch and ward executives, the women’s and youth wings, the Tertiary Education Institutions Network (TEIN), the Zongo Caucus, party elders, patrons and grassroots supporters. He particularly commended the party’s foot soldiers, whose commitment and organisational efforts, he said, contributed to strengthening the NDC’s presence across the region. As the party transitions to a new regional leadership, Dr Amoakohene urged constituency and regional executives who retained their positions to intensify their efforts and work closely with the incoming leadership. He also offered words of encouragement to those who lost their positions in the elections, assuring them that their contributions and sacrifices would remain part of the party’s progress. “To those who unfortunately lost: you will not be forgotten. Your sacrifice is part of everything we built,” he stated.

items.title: 2027: Atiku storms Bauchi communities, questions Tinubu’s grassroots outreach
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA — Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar weekend took his presidential campaign to communities across Bauchi State, drawing large crowds along his route from the airport to the Bauchi State Presidential Lodge and during a road trip to Azare. The tour, which featured a campaign rally, visits to four communities and courtesy calls on two traditional rulers, was part of his efforts to deepen grassroots engagement ahead of the 2027 general elections, while challenging President Bola Tinubu’s record of direct engagement with Nigerians. Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, said Atiku began the day’s engagements at 8am with consultations with stakeholders before proceeding to an 11am rally in Bauchi. Atiku thanked residents for the reception, saying it had strengthened his resolve to take his message of affordable living and responsible leadership to communities across the country. After the rally, his campaign train travelled by road to Azare, stopping in Soro, Kari, Darazo and Misau, where residents turned out to welcome him and his entourage. In Misau, Atiku paid a courtesy visit to the Emir, Alhaji Ahmed Suleiman, thanking him and his council for their hospitality and words of encouragement. He also acknowledged residents who waited to receive his entourage despite its arrival at nightfall. He arrived in Azare at 10.30pm, where he paid a courtesy visit to the Emir of Katagum, extending his engagements with traditional rulers and community leaders. The campaign team is expected to proceed to Potiskum on Sunday for another rally. However, the ADC campaign used the reported scale of the reception to question Tinubu’s grassroots engagement, challenging the President to demonstrate a similar willingness to meet Nigerians directly. “The scale of yesterday’s welcome raises a simple question: can the sitting President volunteer to meet the people and make even half the effort Atiku has made to reach them?” Shaibu said. The post 2027: Atiku storms Bauchi communities, questions Tinubu’s grassroots outreach appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: State Police: NASS to transmit bill to Tinubu this week -Senator Bamidele
items.description: *Raises vital questions on the irresponsible use of social media *Receives ‘The Sun Senator of the Year’ Award *Dedicates award to God, President Tinubu, and 108 other senators By Henry Umoru ABUJA – LEADER of the Senate, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, APC, Ekiti Central has disclosed that the National Assembly will this week the State Police Bill to President Bola Tinubu for assent. He said the National Assembly is expecting four State Houses of Assembly to turn in their reports on or before the National Assembly reconvenes on November 17, 2026, saying with this development, next week is going to be decisive and defining in the National Assembly. Bamidele said whether the remaining states turn in their reports or not, the National must move forward and fulfil the aspiration of the people. According to Bamidele, the principle of proactive lawmaking guided the resolve of the National Assembly to pass the State Police (Constitution Alteration) Bill, which, according to him, proposed the creation of a Federal Police Service and State Police Services. The proposed constitutional amendment which is part of ongoing efforts to restructure Nigeria’s policing architecture by providing for the establishment of State Police Services, is intended to create the constitutional foundation for decentralised policing, amid continuing national discussions on how to strengthen security arrangements and improve responses to security challenges across the country. Bamidele spoke after he received “The Sun Senator of the Year” Award for efficiently managing the business of the parliament and for his proactive approach to lawmaking, which has guided all the undertakings of the Senate since its inauguration in June 2023. In a statement from his Media Directorate on Sunday, the Senate Leader further explained that the creation of the state police service had moved from rhetoric to reality after more than 15 years of unsuccessful attempts to reform the country’s police system. As shown in the records of the National Assembly, Bamidele revealed that no fewer than 32 State Houses of Assembly “have approved the State Police (Constitution Alteration) Bill, 2026. With this, we have successfully crossed the constitutional threshold under Section 9(2) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended). “We are now expecting four State Houses of Assembly to turn in their reports on or before the National Assembly reconvenes on November 17, 2026. This suggests that next week is going to be decisive and defining in the National Assembly. Whether the remaining states turn in their reports or not, we must move forward and fulfil the aspiration of our people. “We are now under obligation to transmit the State Police (Constitution Alteration) Bill, 2026 to the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, His Excellency Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, for assent. This is a responsibility we must consciously discharge on behalf of our constituents and in the interest of national peace, progress, and stability,” he explained further. Contrary to critics of the State Police bill, Bamidele clarified that the initiative was not designed to create ethnic or state armies, but was about establishing state-led, community-anchored policing within clear constitutional safeguards. The Senate leader said as the parliament of the people, the National Assembly had pursued, consciously and conscientiously, people-centred legislation that had direct bearing on the welfare of citizens. Recall that on November 4th, the Senate announced that the proposed State Police system had crossed a major constitutional hurdle, with 30 State Houses of Assembly approving the amendment required to pave the way for its establishment, remaining six others yet to forward theirs to the National Assembly for onward transmission to the President for subsequent assent. As at November 4th, the six states that were yet to Approve the bill for onward transmission to the National Assembly were Kano, Cross River, Abia, Niger, Benue and Oyo. The Senate however gave the six State Houses of Assembly yet to communicate their positions on the proposed constitutional amendment establishing State Police until November 15 to do so, warning that failure to respond by the deadline could be deemed as withholding approval. The remaining six states were expected to communicate their decisions before November 15, when the National Assembly intends to forward the proposed constitutional amendment to President Bola Tinubu for subsequent. The development brought the proposed restructuring of Nigeria’s policing system closer to the final stage of the constitutional amendment process, with presidential assent expected after the National Assembly completes the necessary procedures. Disclosing this penultimate week while updating lawmakers on the progress of consultations with the 36 state legislatures on the proposed amendment, the Senate Leader had said the number of approvals had exceeded the constitutionally required two-thirds of the 36 state legislatures. According to him, for the process to be rounded off, it has to be in three phases with the National Assembly expected to pass the bill, the approval by at least two-thirds of the state legislature and the President to sign the bill into law, adding that the National Assembly had fulfilled its responsibility by passing the bill and transmitting it to all 36 State Houses of Assembly for consideration and approval. Bamidele then said, “Let me explain again, for the avoidance of doubt, three keywords are used in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, as amended. The first word is passage, the second word is approval and the third word is assent. “The reason the writers of our Constitution, our forefathers, put all these specific words is to ensure that no part of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria can be easily amended without the buying in of all the critical stakeholders at all levels of governance. “The passage of the bill was the responsibility of the National Assembly, and that has been completed. Approval is required from at least two-thirds of the 36 State Houses of Assembly in the country, while assent must subsequently be given by the President to complete the constitutional amendment process. The Senate Leader explained that the constitutional requirements were deliberately designed to ensure that amendments to the nation’s supreme law enjoyed the participation and agreement of critical stakeholders across the different levels of government. Bamidele stressed that the 30 approvals already received were significantly above the constitutional requirement of 24 states, describing the development as evidence of widespread support for the proposed reform. “Two important points need to be emphasised. First, we needed the approval of at least two-thirds of the states for this constitutional amendment to proceed. “Two things that need to be emphasised here is that we needed two-thirds of the states at the very least for this to pass, and already two-thirds will be 24. So, as of yet, we already got 30 states, showing the popularity of this bill among Nigerians through the elected representatives in the State Houses of Assembly,” he said. The 30 states that as at that week approved the proposal are Adamawa, Akwa Ibom, Anambra, Bauchi, Bayelsa, Borno, Delta, Ebonyi, Edo, Ekiti, Enugu, Gombe, Imo, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi, Kogi, Kwara, Lagos, Nasarawa, Ogun, Ondo, Osun, Plateau, Rivers, Sokoto, Taraba, Yobe and Zamfara. According to the statement from his Media Office on Sunday, Bamidele who explained how the National Assembly championed the Student Loan (Access to Higher Education) Act, 2024, which replaced a restrictive regime with an inclusive, technology-driven, interest-free loan scheme, said through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), according to him, over ₦204 billion has been disbursed to applicants across 89 colleges, 108 polytechnics, and 126 universities nationwide, adding that rhe Fund has significantly reduced the rate of dropouts in tertiary institutions. He said. “We also championed the National Social Investment Programmes Act, 2023, which gave statutory backing, coordination, and accountability to our social protection system, for poverty reduction, economic inclusion, and social welfare for vulnerable Nigerians. “With the utmost sense of responsibility, we passed the Minimum Wage (Amendment) Act, 2024; Tax Reform Acts, 2025; Investments and Securities Act, 2025; Electoral Act, 2026; Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act, 2024; and Regional Development Commissions Acts, among others. Each of these laws has transformed our economy, strengthened public finance, and deepened electoral credibility,” Bamidele said as he rolled out the achievements of the parliament. While thanking the media for serving as formidable partners in deepening the country’s democracy, Bamidele reaffirmed his commitment “to press freedom, an open parliament, and continuous engagement with journalists. But we must work together to define the responsible use of social media.” He raised highly fundamental questions about the devastating activities of some individuals on social media, noting: “We have seen characters assassinated. We have seen public institutions blackmailed. We have watched people deliberately distort facts. We have seen people unjustifiably peddling lies. We cannot fold our hands and allows this illegality to continue. “I have been a victim of these outlawed activities at different times. I know many Nigerians have been victims as well. But the urgent questions are: Should we leave unregulated this space that define our lives in the decades to come? Or do we prefer a space where characters are assassinated daily, lies peddled, and public institutions unjustifiably discredited? “These are questions that key media actors – Newspaper Proprietors’ Association of Nigeria, Broadcasting Organisations of Nigeria, Nigerian Guild of Editors, and Nigeria Union of Journalists – must honestly answer in this age of information technology. Otherwise, we must all brace up for the consequences of our inability to act at the time that matters most. “We all know that information is critical to our national development as much as to our internal stability. Obviously, this suggests that the way we disseminate information, whether through the traditional or social media, must be well guided by international best practices. “This further suggests that information must be disseminated objectively and responsibly with the intention to inform and not disinform; build and not destroy; develop and not blackmail.” Speaking on the award from Sun Newspapers, Bamidele, however, noted that the award was not a personal achievement or trophy, but purely a validation of collective responsibility, thereby dedicating it to Almighty God, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, 108 other senators, and his constituents, who entrusted him with their mandates. According to the statement, ” He received the award Friday night from the Founder of The Sun Publishing Limited and Chairman of the South East Development Commission, Senator Orji Uzor Kalu, accompanied by several serving senators, governors (serving and former), and his political associates from Ekiti and Lagos States. “Among others, former Ogun State Governor, Chief Olusegun Osoba; his predecessor and Chairman, Senate Committee on Navy, Senator Gbenga Daniel; Chairman, Senate Committee on Banking, Insurance and Other Financial Institutions, Senator Adetokunbo Abiru; Chairman, Senate Committee on Works, Senator Patrick Ndubueze; and Chairman, Senate Committee on the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure, Senator Francis Onyewuchi, accompanied Bamidele to receive the honour. While thanking The Sun Publishing Limited for conferring the prestigious honour on him, Bamidele emphasised again the need to judge the National Assembly not by the volume of bills passed into law, but by the impact of its initiatives on the lives of the people. He said: “I believe in proactive lawmaking. I believe Nigeria must move from reactive governance to proactive governance. I believe our laws must be evidence-based, efficiently implemented, effectively monitored, periodically reviewed, and ultimately measured by their impact on citizens. “I believe that separation of powers is not about hostility, but synergy; not grandstanding, but collaboration; not dissension, but interdependence among the arms of government. I have served most dutifully in the Senate with independence, but at the same time with constructive engagement with other arms because our collective responsibility is national development, peace, and security.” The post State Police: NASS to transmit bill to Tinubu this week -Senator Bamidele appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: When even your Traffic Fine is a scam!
items.description: By Jimmy Aglah Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, the government decided that Ghanaian motorists had enjoyed too much freedom on the roads. Some drove as though speed limits were recommendations from elderly relatives, deserving respectful consideration but not necessarily obedience. Others regarded traffic lights as Christmas decorations, beautiful to behold but entirely optional. The authorities therefore introduced electronic traffic enforcement, hoping cameras would accomplish what policemen, road signs and decades of public education had struggled to achieve. It was a brilliant idea. Cameras do not accept apologies, recognise party colours or appreciate the significance of a driver’s uncle being a Deputy Minister. They simply record offences and leave the authorities to do the rest. Unfortunately, the Republic’s fraudsters were also watching. And being patriotic citizens with an extraordinary appetite for business opportunities, they apparently decided that government should not enjoy a monopoly over the collection of money from frightened motorists. Thus was born Ghana’s newest potential growth industry: Traffic Fine Entrepreneurship. For years, our enterprising fraudsters concentrated on traditional sectors of the deception economy. They promised unsuspecting citizens foreign visas, miraculous investments, parcels of gold and romantic relationships with wealthy strangers who mysteriously required financial assistance before declaring their undying love. But every industry must innovate or perish. Why promise somebody an inheritance from a dead millionaire in London when you can simply inform him that his Toyota Corolla has offended the Republic? No complicated love story. No inheritance documents. Just a threatening message, an alleged traffic offence and instructions to pay before trouble arrives. The Ghana Police Service warned motorists about fraudulent traffic penalty notices on 4 November 2026, while the Cyber Security Authority followed on 9 November with concerns about fake messages and payment websites. Evidently, some people had discovered that where government establishes a collection system, unofficial competitors may soon arrive with their own invoices. In the Republic of Uncommon Sense, even criminality believes in public-private partnership. Consider the predicament of the ordinary Ghanaian motorist. He leaves home determined to obey every traffic regulation. At the first junction, a taxi overtakes him from the wrong side. At the next, an aboboyaa carrying enough merchandise to establish a branch of Kejetia Market passes him with the confidence of a presidential convoy. Before reaching his destination, three motorcycles have demonstrated that road markings are merely artistic expressions on asphalt. Our gentleman, meanwhile, is doing 50 kilometres per hour, glancing nervously at his speedometer as though it contains the examination results of his firstborn. Then his telephone announces the arrival of a traffic penalty. Ei! He checks the message, his registration number and his memory. Was it yesterday? Last Tuesday? Perhaps the day he accelerated slightly to escape an impatient truck whose driver appeared to believe that brakes were invented for cowards. The message demands payment. But is it genuine? One friend advises him to ignore it. Another warns that failure to pay could lead to prosecution. A third suggests visiting the police station. A fourth, who considers himself an expert in digital governance because he once successfully renewed his passport online, recommends checking the official platform. By the time our motorist finishes his consultations, he has spent enough airtime to finance a small telecommunications company. And he still cannot establish whether he owes the Republic money or whether the Republic’s unofficial business community is attempting to collect a private tax. What a country! Our ancestors warned that when two elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers. In modern Ghana, however, the elephants have discovered mobile money, and the grass is being asked to enter its PIN. The tragedy is that electronic traffic enforcement is not inherently a bad idea. Ghana’s roads have witnessed enough recklessness to convince even the most stubborn optimist that something must change. We cannot continue treating road safety as a seasonal sermon delivered during Christmas and Easter, only to return afterwards to the national sport of overtaking death at dangerous bends. But technology without adequate public education can become an elaborate invitation to confusion. When motorists are uncertain about how official notices are delivered, where penalties should be verified and which payment channels are legitimate, fraudsters need little imagination. They merely dress deception in the respectable clothing of government authority and wait for frightened citizens to open their wallets. As the elders say, when the owner of the house fails to identify his children, the stranger may enter the compound and demand supper. Indeed, perhaps the Republic should introduce a compulsory examination for motorists: Advanced Traffic Fine Authentication. Question One: You receive a message claiming that your vehicle exceeded the speed limit. What should you do? A. Pay immediately before the police arrest your ancestors. B. Forward the message to your family WhatsApp group for collective interpretation. C. Consult your pastor to determine whether the offence is physical or spiritual. D. Verify the notice through the officially authorised channel. Naturally, the correct answer is D. Unfortunately, in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, many citizens may have exhausted A, B and C before discovering D. And therein lies the serious matter beneath the laughter. The success of electronic enforcement depends not merely on detecting wrongdoing but also on public confidence. A genuine penalty must be distinguishable from a fraudulent demand without requiring the investigative resources of EOCO, the patience of Job and the technical expertise of a cybersecurity consultant. Government must make verification simple, publicise authorised payment channels and ensure suspicious notices can be reported without unnecessary bureaucracy. Otherwise, motorists may ignore legitimate penalties because they suspect fraud, while others pay criminals because they fear prosecution. The criminal wins either way. Perhaps the greatest irony is that the Republic has invested in technology to detect motorists exceeding speed limits, only to discover that fraudsters are equally determined to overtake the enforcement system in the race for the motorist’s money. And so, in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, government is pursuing speeding motorists, fraudsters are pursuing frightened motorists, and frightened motorists are pursuing somebody who can explain which pursuit is legitimate. Perhaps the next generation of traffic cameras should be programmed to detect not only speeding vehicles but also speeding fraudsters. For in a country where even a traffic fine can be counterfeit, the only thing travelling faster than the motorist is the criminal’s imagination. And unlike the unfortunate driver, that imagination appears to have no speed limit.

items.title: Musulmans de France : entre le souci du détail et le sens des priorités
items.description: Depuis l’entrée en vigueur des dispositifs de lutte contre le « séparatisme », l’accumulation de mesures administratives visant les institutions musulmanes en France dessine une tendance de fond, qui suscite de nombreuses interrogations : des opérations de contrôle ont été menées, aboutissant à la fermeture de plusieurs mosquées ou salles de prière, à l’expulsion de dizaines d’imams et de prédicateurs, ainsi qu’à la fermeture ou à la dissolution de nombreuses associations culturelles et d’enseignement de la langue arabe. Dans le domaine éducatif, cette pression s’est également traduite par des décisions visant des établissements privés sous contrat, notamment des écoles et lycées musulmans . Des décisions qui fragilisent les structures éducatives, culturelles et cultuelles des musulmans de France Plusieurs établissements scolaires musulmans ont perdu leur contrat d’association avec l’État, fragilisant leur financement public et leur avenir. Cette situation pourrait, à terme, conduire à la fermeture de certaines de ces structures. Si les pouvoirs publics justifient ces mesures par la défense des principes républicains, plusieurs juristes et responsables associatifs alertent sur leurs conséquences pour les structures éducatives, culturelles et cultuelles des musulmans de France. Pourtant, sur les réseaux sociaux notamment, une grande partie des discussions au sein de la communauté musulmane continue de se concentrer sur des questions qui, bien qu’importantes sur le plan individuel, occupent un espace disproportionné : viande halal, la présence d’alcool ou de gélatine dans certains produits, les normes vestimentaires, les horaires de prière ou encore le statut de la musique. Ces sujets alimentent des polémiques interminables, tandis que les véritables enjeux collectifs peinent à susciter la même mobilisation. Ce décalage devrait nous interpeller. D’un côté, des institutions sont fragilisées et des espaces essentiels de transmission disparaissent ; de l’autre, nous consacrons une énergie considérable à des débats relevant souvent de choix personnels, d’interprétations religieuses ou de divergences d’opinions. L’enjeu n’est pas d’éluder ces questions, dont certaines touchent légitimement à la pratique cultuelle, mais de refuser qu’elles monopolisent l’attention au détriment des combats décisifs pour notre avenir collectif. Les véritables enjeux Il ne s’agit nullement d’opposer la foi à l’engagement citoyen, ni de renoncer à nos principes religieux, mais simplement de retrouver le sens des priorités. À quoi bon multiplier les controverses sur les détails du quotidien si nous demeurons incapables de nous mobiliser pour préserver les écoles de nos enfants, défendre nos lieux de culte et soutenir les associations qui assurent la transmission de notre patrimoine spirituel ? Les prescriptions religieuses conservent naturellement toute leur légitimité. Mais elles ne doivent pas occulter des enjeux autrement plus déterminants : la défense des libertés fondamentales, l’éducation de nos jeunes, la pérennité de nos institutions et la structuration de notre tissu associatif. À l'heure où les musulmans de France participent pleinement à la vie économique, sociale et culturelle du pays, défendre leurs droits, préserver leurs structures et faire entendre leur voix ne relève en rien d'un repli communautaire, mais d'une exigence strictement démocratique. Le temps est venu d’opérer un changement de cap : substituer aux controverses stériles une réflexion stratégique exigeante, ancrée dans la solidarité et l’action collective. Un tel sursaut impose de surmonter les divisions, les rivalités et les querelles d’ego qui minent trop souvent la cohésion des initiatives communes. Une communauté ne se construit pas uniquement autour de prescriptions alimentaires ou de controverses théologiques. Elle se construit aussi par ses écoles, ses lieux de culte, ses associations et sa capacité à préparer l’avenir des générations futures. Le véritable enjeu n’est donc pas de moins parler de religion, mais de faire émerger une conscience collective apte à défendre ses droits, protéger ses institutions et tracer des perspectives durables. Car à force de nous épuiser dans des querelles secondaires, nous risquons de déserter les combats essentiels, et de perdre les espaces mêmes qui nous permettent de vivre, de transmettre et d’incarner notre fois. « À l'heure où les musulmans de France participent pleinement à la vie économique, sociale et culturelle du pays, défendre leurs droits, préserver leurs structures et faire entendre leur voix ne relève en rien d'un repli communautaire, mais d'une exigence strictement démocratique. » Azzédine Gaci, recteur de la mosquée de Villeurbanne L’article Musulmans de France : entre le souci du détail et le sens des priorités est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: ICPC vows to publish recovered assets, disclose owners
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission, ICPC, has pledged to make public details of recovered assets, including their ownership and current status, in a move aimed at strengthening transparency and accountability in Nigeria’s anti-corruption campaign. The commitment comes as African countries seek stronger cooperation to track down and recover wealth stolen through corruption and concealed in foreign jurisdictions, while ensuring that recovered resources are properly managed and used for public benefit. Prince Hassan Mohammed, Director of Special Services at the ICPC and Chairman of the Local Organising Committee of the maiden General Assembly of the African Asset Recovery Practitioners’ Forum, AARP-F, gave the assurance at a pre-conference media briefing in Abuja, weekend. Mohammed, however, could not provide figures on the volume of assets recovered in Nigeria when asked whether the commission had compiled data ahead of the continental gathering scheduled for November 17 to 20 at the Abuja Continental Hotel. On whether the ICPC would periodically disclose recovered assets, their status and ownership details, he said: “Definitely, ICPC will do that. Nothing is hidden. It’s a public document. “Anything recovered is for the public. And so, ICPC will definitely declare anything and whatever has been recovered.” Explaining the rationale behind the African Union-backed initiative, Mohammed said asset recovery had become an integral part of the global fight against corruption, stressing that retrieving stolen wealth was only part of the responsibility. He said recovered assets must ultimately benefit citizens rather than merely be recorded as successes by anti-corruption agencies. “To be sure, to ensure that what was recovered is put to use for the benefit of the generality of the masses is an aspect of the fight against corruption, which the African Union is advancing,” he said. On whether any African country was ahead of Nigeria in asset recovery, Mohammed said it was difficult to make such comparisons because some countries did not publicly disclose their recoveries. “Some of these countries recover their assets and you don’t know what they have recovered. We don’t know whether they are doing their recoveries or not,” he said. He said continental engagements such as the Abuja Assembly would provide opportunities for countries to exchange experiences and discuss their respective recovery efforts. In his address, Mohammed said the four-day Assembly would bring together representatives of 54 African countries, alongside international partners and other stakeholders, to strengthen cooperation and develop practical strategies for tackling illicit financial flows. Established in Nairobi, Kenya, in April 2025, the AARP-F provides a continental platform for asset recovery practitioners to advance the implementation of the Common African Position on Asset Recovery, CAPAR. The Assembly, themed, ‘From Commitment to Action – Enhancing Africa’s Asset Recovery Architecture through Effective Implementation of the Common African Position on Asset Recovery (CADAR)’, is expected to review progress, address institutional and operational gaps, strengthen cooperation and adopt governance instruments and strategic action plans. Mohammed said participants would also have opportunities to visit locations in Nigeria to assess how some recovered assets were being put to use. He said the meeting would seek to move beyond policy declarations by developing common approaches to information sharing, mutual legal assistance and collaboration among anti-corruption agencies and other relevant institutions. He urged the media to sustain public scrutiny of asset recovery efforts beyond the Abuja meeting, describing journalists as important partners in translating technical discussions and policy commitments into information accessible to ordinary Africans. The Assembly is expected to strengthen Africa’s collective capacity to trace, freeze, confiscate, recover and repatriate illicitly acquired assets, while ensuring that recovered resources contribute to the continent’s development. The post ICPC vows to publish recovered assets, disclose owners appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mahama urges traditional authorities to strengthen role in promoting peace and social cohesion
items.description: President John Mahama has described traditional authorities as indispensable partners in Ghana’s national development, urging them to strengthen their contribution to peace, social cohesion and community development. He said traditional institutions remained critical to addressing some of the country’s challenges, including unemployment, social inequality, land and chieftaincy disputes, environmental degradation and threats to national security. The President made the remarks in an address delivered on his behalf by the Minister for the Interior, Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak, at a ceremony in Sandema in the Upper East Region to mark the 20th anniversary of the passing of the late Nab Dr Ayieta Azantilow. President Mahama said the late traditional ruler demonstrated that traditional leadership must go beyond preserving customs and exercising customary authority to include improving the social and economic conditions of the people. He reaffirmed the government’s commitment to working closely with traditional authorities and other stakeholders to support initiatives aimed at improving living conditions, expanding opportunities for the youth and promoting sustainable development across the country. The President also cautioned the youth against the use of illicit drugs, warning that drug abuse posed a serious threat to their well-being, future prospects and the country’s development. He urged traditional authorities to guide young people towards responsible choices and collaborate with government and other stakeholders to address the problem and protect the younger generation. President Mahama expressed hope that the commemoration would strengthen unity among chiefs and people of the Bulsa Traditional Area and inspire renewed commitment to the development of the area and the Upper East Region. The ceremony also featured the launch of a book in honour of the late traditional ruler, whose nearly 75-year reign was distinguished by contributions to education, healthcare, traditional governance and community development.

items.title: Ghana’s new export miracle: From Cocoa to Cocaine!
items.description: By Jimmy Aglah Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, a country famous for producing cocoa, gold and excellent excuses discovered that its agricultural export industry had acquired a rather mysterious new product. The discovery was not made at the Ministry of Trade, the Ghana Export Promotion Authority or any of those important conferences where distinguished gentlemen gather to discuss value addition over bottled water and meat pies. It was made in Spain, where customs officers opened a consignment of Ghanaian coconuts and discovered that the fruits had apparently travelled with 2.6 tonnes of cocaine. For a nation that has spent decades preaching export diversification, this was an extraordinary development. Our farmers had been encouraged to add value to their produce, but nobody had explained that the value should be hidden beneath the produce in wooden crates. Somewhere along the international supply chain, certain enterprising criminals had evidently taken the government’s economic transformation agenda rather too literally. The humble coconut must have been deeply embarrassed. For generations, it had served humanity faithfully, providing refreshing water, nutritious flesh and occasional employment for young men who could climb trees faster than graduates could find jobs. Now, through no fault of its own, it had become an exhibit in an international narcotics investigation. According to Spanish authorities, two containers loaded at Tema Port in August arrived in Valencia later that month. Beneath false bottoms in wooden crates containing coconuts, investigators discovered approximately 2.6 tonnes of cocaine. The consignment was subsequently tracked to Almería, where two men were arrested. The operation was publicly announced on 11 November 2026. The Spanish officers must have wondered what extraordinary agricultural technology had enabled Ghanaian coconuts to acquire such expensive foundations. A coconut ordinarily contains water, flesh and a hard shell. These particular coconuts had apparently been provided with an underground economy. And this was hardly the first time Ghanaian commodities had found themselves in such distinguished criminal company. Timber had featured in an enormous cocaine seizure in Amsterdam. Cassava flour had attracted the attention of Belgian authorities. Gari sacks had appeared in a domestic narcotics interception. Even plastic waste, which sensible nations are desperately trying to recycle, had reportedly been recruited into the international drug business. At this rate, Ghana may soon require a new department at the Export Promotion Authority: the Directorate of Unintended Value Addition. One can imagine the next international trade exhibition. Ghanaian exporters arrive proudly displaying their products. The timber merchants arrange their wood, the cassava processors exhibit their flour, and the coconut farmers carefully polish their fruits. Then a mysterious gentleman wearing dark glasses approaches the exhibition organisers and enquires whether there is sufficient space beneath the tables. Our innocent exporters may soon have to attach sworn affidavits to every shipment, declaring that their cassava is merely cassava, their coconut contains nothing more exciting than coconut water, and their timber has no ambition to become an international narcotics courier. But before we condemn our agricultural produce, let us remember that a goat does not become a thief merely because somebody hides stolen money beneath its sleeping place. The cocaine was concealed by human beings. The coconuts were innocent passengers, unfortunate enough to find themselves travelling with criminals who had mistaken agricultural exports for a branch of organised crime. The more troubling question is how such consignments enter the international shipping system in the first place. Ghana has ports, customs officers, scanners, inspection procedures, intelligence agencies and enough official acronyms to fill a small dictionary. We have institutions responsible for examining cargo, preventing smuggling and protecting the integrity of our borders. Yet the recurring discoveries raise uncomfortable questions about the effectiveness of the arrangements intended to detect illicit shipments. Modern scanning technology can examine containers without requiring an officer to unpack every coconut, count every grain of gari or interrogate every piece of timber. Unfortunately, technology is only as effective as the people and procedures surrounding it. In the investigation arising from the cocaine seizure in France, prosecutors alleged that suspicious scanning images had not been properly examined before the cargo was cleared. Customs officers were among those charged, although the allegations remain subject to judicial determination. Perhaps the Republic requires a new generation of scanners. Not merely machines capable of looking through containers, but machines capable of looking through negligence, compromised procedures and the occasional temptation to look in the opposite direction. Imagine such a device at Tema Port. A container approaches the inspection point. The machine examines its contents and announces: “The cargo contains coconuts, suspicious compartments and three explanations that do not agree with one another.” The officer presses a button to silence the machine. It immediately announces: “Attempt to suppress evidence detected.” Such technology would undoubtedly revolutionise port security, although its manufacturers might struggle to obtain the necessary import permits. But Ghana is not a country that sits idle when confronted with a national emergency. We have developed an impressive administrative tradition of responding to difficult problems with committees, task forces, technical teams, investigative panels and carefully worded assurances that the situation is receiving the highest attention. Following the September cocaine seizure in France, President John Dramani Mahama directed the establishment of an inter-agency task force to develop a roadmap for strengthening border security. The question now is what has happened to that roadmap. Which recommendations have been implemented? Have inspection procedures changed? Are suspicious cargoes receiving more effective scrutiny? And how will the public know whether the reforms are working? The Republic has considerable experience in preparing roadmaps. We have roadmaps for development, roadmaps for economic transformation and roadmaps for institutional reform. What occasionally defeats us is the inconvenient expectation that somebody must actually travel along the road. A roadmap that remains in a filing cabinet is merely a tourist attraction for documents. And while the security agencies investigate the cocaine, our politicians have discovered another valuable national resource: political ammunition. In Ghana, every scandal has two lives. The first concerns what actually happened. The second concerns which political party can extract the greatest advantage from the happening. The opposition has demanded accountability over the recurring seizures, including changes in security leadership. Government officials and security authorities have pointed to enforcement efforts and the wider history of the country’s narcotics challenges. The spectacle is familiar enough to qualify as a national cultural festival. When a political party occupies the opposition benches, every kilogramme of intercepted cocaine becomes evidence of an alarming failure of governance. When the same party occupies the government benches, the matter suddenly acquires historical complexity, international dimensions and a pressing need for citizens to avoid premature conclusions. The cocaine itself remains politically neutral. It does not carry an NDC membership card or an NPP polling-station executive’s identification. It does not attend party congresses, wear campaign T-shirts or contribute to manifesto preparation. Yet the moment it is discovered, politicians rush to claim custody of the narrative. If cocaine could speak, it might complain that it had entered the international trade system illegally but was now being used for perfectly legal political arguments. Accountability, however, should not change its meaning whenever political parties exchange seats. A proverb reminds us that the man who complains about smoke from his neighbour’s kitchen should first examine the firewood burning in his own. And beyond the political exchanges lies another victim of this unfortunate national embarrassment: the honest Ghanaian exporter. Somewhere in the countryside, a coconut farmer wakes before sunrise, tends his trees, harvests his produce and struggles to find a buyer willing to pay a fair price. He knows nothing about cocaine trafficking, international criminal syndicates or concealed compartments in shipping containers. Yet every major seizure involving agricultural consignments risks casting suspicion on legitimate trade, encouraging additional scrutiny and imposing costs on innocent exporters. The coconut farmer wants his produce to reach a supermarket. The criminal wants the same coconut to reach a warehouse where nobody will ask too many questions about what lies beneath it. We must resist the temptation to conclude that every shipment intercepted abroad proves that Ghanaian security officers were compromised. International drug trafficking involves multiple countries, complex shipping arrangements and opportunities for concealment. Establishing where drugs were inserted and which safeguards failed requires evidence rather than political imagination. Nevertheless, the questions remain. Who owns these consignments? Who verifies the exporters? How are containers secured? What happens when scanners identify suspicious images? And what consequences follow when investigations establish negligence or criminal complicity? These are questions that cannot be answered by arresting the coconut. Perhaps the next time Ghana participates in an international agricultural exhibition, the organisers should provide a special pavilion where our innocent commodities can hold a press conference to defend their reputations. The cassava will insist that it has always been flour. The gari will demand an apology for the unfortunate publicity. The timber will remind journalists that it was cut down against its will. And the coconut, speaking on behalf of the entire agricultural community, will declare that it has never knowingly participated in the international narcotics trade. We have spent decades trying to convince the world that Ghanaian agricultural products deserve a place on international supermarket shelves. Now, thanks to certain criminal enterprises, some of those products are finding their way onto international police evidence tables. The coconut has committed no offence. The cassava is innocent. The gari has an impeccable character. Even the timber has refused to make a statement without its lawyer. Perhaps it is time we stopped interrogating the agricultural produce and started examining the human beings who keep giving it criminal travelling companions. For when the same farm keeps producing strange harvests, the wise farmer does not arrest the crops. He investigates who has been planting the seeds.

items.title: US flight disruptions: Trump admin says air travel chaos may last another day
items.description: The Trump administration said Sunday the air travel havoc triggered by a no-takeoff order could drag on for another day, pushing back its timetable for a return to normal. Hundreds more flights were cancelled and questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world’s largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess. Officials blame Friday’s huge snafu on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables. President Donald Trump on Sunday ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle. Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America’s outdated air traffic control system. “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration. “Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” Trump asserted. FAA chief Bryan Bedford had said Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday. But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travelers to where they need to be. “So, in the airspace, we’re going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow,” Duffy said on ABC News. “We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that.” – ‘I’m the secretary’ – Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure, such as, he said, radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s. “So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I’m the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me,” Duffy said in an interview on CNN. As of Sunday morning 1,460 flights within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled, according to the travel monitor site flightaware.com. The Trump administration has blamed Friday’s ground stop — meaning no planes can take off — on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines. Friday’s disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace, which is among the busiest in the world, since the 9/11 attacks. The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, it also raised serious concerns about the country’s aging infrastructure. Duffy has appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to “meet this moment.” But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump’s Republicans could already have done this. items.title: Guinea deports 1,557 West Africans in gold mining crackdown
items.description: By Favour Ulebor & Agency Reports Guinea has expelled 1,557 West African nationals arrested and convicted for illegal gold mining as the government intensifies its crackdown on unauthorised mining activities across the country. Judicial and security sources told AFP on Sunday that the foreigners, mostly from Burkina Faso and Mali, were arrested at different mining sites during an operation against illegal mining. The deportees were transported in a convoy of 44 vehicles, which arrived in Kouremale, a border town between Guinea and Mali, on Saturday after leaving the capital, Conakry, on Friday. According to the sources, the foreigners were released and expelled after receiving prison sentences ranging from 18 months to two years. The Guinean government has increased operations against illegal gold mining since the beginning of November, particularly in Siguiri, a major gold-producing region in the northeastern part of the country. Authorities said the crackdown was aimed at stopping the illegal exploitation of mineral resources and reducing the environmental damage caused by unregulated mining. The operations have also affected thousands of West African migrants who travelled to Guinea in search of employment and better living conditions after fleeing poverty and insecurity in their home countries. Meanwhile, the crackdown has sparked tensions between miners and security forces. At least 10 people were killed on Wednesday following violent clashes between miners and security personnel in Siguiri, according to a government statement issued on Thursday. Reacting to the deaths, Guinea’s main opposition coalition on Saturday condemned what it described as an “authoritarian drift” and criticised the government’s use of force “as a method of government.” The latest expulsions come amid growing concerns over the treatment of migrant miners and the government’s efforts to control illegal mining activities. items.title: African oil producers urged to balance local content with investment
items.description: African oil-producing countries have been urged to strengthen local content development by creating a sustainable pipeline of upstream investments and projects, while maintaining an enabling business environment that attracts international investors. The call was made at just ended Local Content Conference and Exhibition (LCCE), where industry stakeholders stressed that building a resilient, competitive and sustainable oil and gas sector requires more than policies promoting indigenous participation. It also demands continuous exploration, new project development and strategic partnerships capable of generating lasting opportunities for local businesses. Contributing to a panel discussion on enhancing local content for sustainable growth, Deputy Managing Director of Eni Ghana, Mr Baluri Kassim Bukari, said Ghana’s experience demonstrated that local content development was intrinsically linked to the level of activity and investment within the upstream sector. He cited Ghana’s Offshore Cape Three Points (OCTP) project, operated by Eni Ghana, which currently supplies more than 70 per cent of the country’s domestic gas for power generation, as an example of how upstream investments could generate significant opportunities for indigenous businesses. Mr Bukari recalled that during the project’s development phase, several international companies entered Ghana, established joint ventures with local partners and secured contracts under the country’s local content framework. He disclosed that Eni Ghana awarded more than US$4 billion in contracts to local companies, including indigenous businesses and joint ventures, generating employment and stimulating economic activity. He noted that Takoradi experienced a significant increase in commercial activity during the development phase, with hotels and other businesses benefiting from the presence of companies and workers engaged in the project. However, economic activity slowed following the completion of the development phase, leaving many local businesses with fewer opportunities. According to him, this experience highlights a fundamental requirement for successful local content development: a sustained pipeline of upstream investments and projects. “You can’t have local content without content,” he said, urging Ghana to accelerate the award of petroleum blocks, encourage exploration and facilitate the development of new projects. Mr Bukari cautioned against a situation where indigenous companies obtain regulatory permits, establish offices and employ workers but struggle to secure contracts because of insufficient industry activity. He stressed the need for Ghana to move beyond memoranda of understanding (MOUs) towards concrete agreements backed by firm investment commitments and Final Investment Decisions (FIDs). On the capacity of indigenous companies, he observed that opportunities existed across the entire oil and gas value chain, although certain specialised activities required advanced technologies and technical competencies that were not yet fully developed locally. He therefore called for deliberate investment in technical training, health and safety, operational standards and other specialised skills to strengthen the capacity of Ghanaian companies to compete for more complex industry assignments. In highlighting local business participation, Mr Bukari emphasized the broader economic contribution of OCTP, particularly the supply of gas to the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) for domestic thermal power generation. He noted that the gas continued to support electricity supply to households, schools, churches, commercial establishments and industries. Deputy Chief Executive for Finance, Commercial and Administration of GNPC, Mr Hamis Yussif, said Ghana’s local content strategy had been shaped by the need to attract international partners while progressively developing indigenous capabilities. He explained that following the discovery of oil, GNPC’s accelerated growth strategy identified local content development as one of its key priorities. He said Ghana’s ambition should extend beyond local employment and procurement to building indigenous companies capable of owning assets, developing technical expertise and competing in international markets. Achieving this, he noted, would require sustained investment and a consistent pipeline of opportunities to enable local businesses to maintain, strengthen and expand their capabilities. Mr Yussif cautioned, however, against viewing local content and foreign investment as competing objectives, stressing that without projects and investments from international oil companies, opportunities for indigenous businesses to participate in the industry would remain limited. Sharing Nigeria’s experience, Eng. Bashir Ahmed, a representative of the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), underscored the importance of adapting local content policies to changing industry conditions. He explained that Nigeria’s local content framework became more structured following the establishment of the NCDMB in 2010, after earlier policies failed to achieve the desired results. Nigeria initially pursued an aggressive local content strategy, which contributed to the development of domestic fabrication, engineering and manufacturing capabilities. Eng. Ahmed cited the integration of topside modules in Nigeria around 2013 as a significant milestone, alongside the growth of local manufacturers providing goods and services to the oil and gas industry. However, he noted that the subsequent slowdown in major deepwater projects exposed the challenges of building local capacity without corresponding industry activity. Although Nigerian companies had invested in fabrication facilities and engineering capabilities, the absence of new investment decisions by international oil companies limited the availability of projects and commercial opportunities for local businesses. He said Nigeria subsequently reviewed its approach through executive orders, regulatory adjustments and tax incentives introduced around 2022 and 2023, with the aim of making its local content framework more supportive of investment while sustaining the country’s indigenous participation objectives. Representing Angola, Ms Maura Nunes of the National Agency for Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG) said the country’s local content policy was anchored on the principle of “For Angolans, by Angolans, with Angolans.” She explained that a presidential decree introduced in 2020 established two principal objectives: increasing the participation of Angolan companies in the oil and gas industry and developing the skills and capabilities of the country’s human resources. The panel discussion was moderated by the Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Upstream Chamber, Mr David Ampofo.

items.title: Ghana proposes six-point declaration to reform AU financing
items.description: Ghana has proposed a six-point declaration to strengthen the financing of the African Union, calling on member states to move beyond discussions and commit to concrete measures to secure the Union’s financial future. The proposal, known as the Accra Declaration on Financing the Union, was presented by Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa at the 27th Extraordinary Session of the AU Executive Council on Financing the African Union in Accra. The proposed declaration outlines six commitments, including; First, we endorse the integrated pathway (Option C) as our preferred model for financing and reform. Second, we commit each Member State to implementing the levy or an equivalent predictable and verifiable domestic mechanism, supported by transparent rules and reporting. Third, we adopt a unified programme-based budget, a medium-term expenditure framework, and the principle of one programme, one budget line. Fourth, we will capitalise the Peace Fund to reach the USD 1 billion target and establish a replenishment mechanism. Fifth, we endorse and institutionalise the African Union’s partnership with the Alliance of African Multilateral Financial Institutions. Sixth, we commit to reviewing contribution arrangements, including the contribution cap and the erosion of real value. Mr Ablakwa said Ghana wanted the session to produce concrete commitments rather than end with discussions alone. “Let this Session be remembered not for what we said, but for what we signed,” he told delegates. Under the proposal, member states would endorse the integrated pathway, known as Option C, as the preferred model for financing and reforming the African Union. They would also commit to implementing the levy on eligible imports or introducing an equivalent predictable and verifiable domestic financing mechanism, backed by transparent rules and reporting. The declaration further proposes a unified programme-based budget, a medium-term expenditure framework and the principle of one programme, one budget line. On the Peace Fund, Ghana wants member states to commit to raising its capitalisation to the US$1 billion target and establishing a replenishment mechanism to sustain it. The proposal also calls for the institutionalisation of the African Union’s partnership with the Alliance of African Multilateral Financial Institutions and a review of contribution arrangements, including the contribution cap and the erosion of the real value of contributions. As part of efforts to advance the proposals, Ghana will convene an Extraordinary Summit on African Financial Institutions in Accra in 2027, when it assumes the chairmanship of the African Union. Mr Ablakwa said the summit would be a decisive opportunity for the continent to commit to building, capitalising and operationalising its financial institutions. He also called on the AU Commission to prepare a time-bound implementation framework ahead of the summit, with clearly assigned responsibilities, deadlines, milestones and reporting arrangements. The minister said the proposed declaration must also reflect the interests of women, young people and underrepresented groups. “An inclusive Union must also be adequately financed. We will evaluate every decision in this Declaration for its impact on women, young people, and underrepresented groups. Africa’s young people are not spectators in this conversation; they are its very purpose,” he said.

items.title: Adeleke demotes Osun traditional rulers over pro APC stance
items.description: By Shina Abubakar Osogbo The Governor Ademola Adeleke-led administration in Osun State has demoted two traditional rulers, the Alagunbeelewo of Agunbeelewo and the Olu of Irepodun, in Osogbo, the State capital. The demotion of the part 2 traditional rulers was contained in a letter by the Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, dated November 5, signed for the Permanent Secretary by one Wale Alliyu and copied the Ataoja of Osogbo. The two separate letters addressed to the affected monarchs, stated that the State Executive Council presided over by the Governor on October 23rd has approved their de-recognise their stools as part 2 traditional rulers back to that minor chieftaincy. “I am directed to inform you that the State Executive Council ably led by His Excellency Senator Ademola Jackson Nurudeen Adeleke has approved the de-recognition of your stool as Part II (Recognized) stool under the Chief’s Law (Cap, 25) Laws of Osun State, 2002 with effect from 23rd October, 2026. “By this de-recognition, your stool now reverts to a Minor Chieftaincy to which Part III of the Chief’s Law applies and consequently, all the rights, privileges and allowances being enjoyed as a recognized Chief will by this development cease. Although the letter did not state any reason for the demotion but the Alagunbeelewo of Agunbeelewo, Chief Maruf Olayiwola disclosed that they were both alleged of associating with the APC instead of the Accord party in the state. “It is unfortunate that till now, no one disclosed our offence but we were told that we are not associating with Accord party and we did not collect money from anyone. We have friends in the APC and cannot deny our relationship with them. I believe that is not enough reason to sack us from the stool. “Governor Adeleke should not allow some persons to reduce the office of the Governor to that of settling personal grudges for the sake of posterity”, he said. Meanwhile, a civil society organisation, Local Government Development Initiative (LGDI), berated the State Government for acting lawless over the matter. Its Spokesperson Adeniyi Faith while addressing newsmen in Osogbo on Sunday, counselled the State Government not to politicise traditional institutions in the state to ensure its sanctity. “We wish to remind Governor Adeleke that the power of a state government over traditional institutions is not unlimited. Such powers must be exercised strictly in accordance with the applicable laws, established procedures, principles of natural justice and the constitutional guarantee of fair hearing. “The government must demonstrate the legal authority, procedural compliance and legitimate grounds for every decision it takes concerning the appointment, suspension or removal of a traditional ruler. Political authority must never be mistaken for unlimited authority. “We are not suggesting that traditional rulers are above the law or cannot be removed under any circumstances. However, where the law prescribes procedures for such removal, those procedures must be followed without manipulation, political intimidation or selective application. “Governor Adeleke must understand that traditional rulership is not a toy that he can pick up, throw away or manipulate whenever he feels like doing so. The traditional institution is bigger than any political administration, and its dignity must be preserved beyond the tenure of any governor”, he said. The post Adeleke demotes Osun traditional rulers over pro APC stance appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ablakwa urges AU members to implement 0.2% import levy to fund Union
items.description: Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has urged African Union member states that have not implemented the agreed 0.2 per cent levy on eligible imports to do so without delay to strengthen the Union’s financial independence. He said only 18 of the AU’s 55 member states had implemented the levy, which was agreed in 2016 as a predictable source of funding for the continental body. Speaking at the 27th Extraordinary Session of the Executive Council on Financing the African Union in Accra, Mr Ablakwa said Africa could not continue to depend heavily on external support to finance its priorities. He noted that although member states were projected to fund nearly 99 per cent of the AU’s operational budget in 2027, they contributed only about four per cent of its programme budget and 12 per cent of its peace and security budget. “Put plainly: we pay for the lights, but we ask others to pay for the work,” he said. The Minister called for the adoption of an integrated financing and reform approach that would improve both revenue mobilisation and the management of the Union’s resources. He said the reforms should include eliminating duplication, phasing out overlapping programmes and adopting a unified programme-based budget, a medium-term expenditure framework and the principle of one programme per budget line. Mr Ablakwa also called for a review of the existing $200 million contribution cap and measures to address the erosion of the real value of member states’ contributions. He said Ghana would strengthen efforts to implement the levy domestically and report its progress to the Executive Council. The Minister further proposed an Accra Declaration on Financing the Union, setting out six commitments, including implementation of the levy or an equivalent predictable domestic funding mechanism, adoption of a unified budget framework and increased funding for the AU Peace Fund. He said the reforms were necessary to ensure that the African Union had the resources to fulfil its growing responsibilities. “We cannot expect our Union to take on increasing responsibilities while operating with progressively fewer resources,” he said.

items.title: Francophonie : levée de boucliers en Afrique contre la volonté de Paris d’imposer un candidat européen
items.description: La succession a la tete de l'Organisation internationale de la francophonie (OIF) prend des allures de bras de fer diplomatique entre Paris et plusieurs capitales africaines. a la veille de la designation du prochain secretaire general, prevue le 16 novembre a Phnom Penh, les demarches d'Emmanuel Macron pour favoriser une candidature europeenne suscitent des tensions et ravivent les interrogations sur le poids reel des etats africains dans la gouvernance de l'organisation. Au cœur de la controverse, un courrier adresse par le president francais a son homologue rwandais Paul Kagame, dans la nuit du 12 au 13 novembre. Selon les informations rapportees par Jeune Afrique, Emmanuel Macron aurait demande le retrait de la candidature de Louise Mushikiwabo, en lice pour un troisieme mandat, afin de faciliter l'emergence d'un candidat de compromis : Dacian Ciolos, ancien Premier ministre roumain. L'initiative francaise, confirmee par le ministre rwandais des Affaires etrangeres, Olivier Nduhungirehe, a provoque de vives reactions lors de la Conference ministerielle de la francophonie, organisee le 14 novembre. Le chef de la diplomatie rwandaise a categoriquement ecarte un retrait de sa candidate, affirmant que Kigali ne cederait pas, « encore moins sur injonction ». La reaction de plusieurs delegations africaines traduit un malaise qui depasse la seule rivalite entre candidats. Pour ces representants, la volonte de Paris d'eviter une election au profit d'un arrangement diplomatique revient a peser sur une decision qui appartient aux etats membres. « L'initiative d'Emmanuel Macron est profondement irrespectueuse pour les Africains », a estime un representant africain cite par Jeune Afrique. La souverainete des etats africains au cœur du bras de fer La controverse met en evidence une fracture autour de la methode de designation du prochain secretaire general. Alors que Paris defend un consensus destine a preserver l'unite de l'organisation, plusieurs delegations africaines reclament l'application des regles institutionnelles, qui prevoient un vote lorsque les candidatures ne font pas l'objet d'un accord. Le representant de Djibouti, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, a ainsi rappele que « la meilleure facon pour garder l'unite de l'organisation est d'en respecter les textes ». Une position soutenue notamment par les delegations ivoirienne, gabonaise et camerounaise. En face, la Roumanie, la Macedoine du Nord, Andorre et Monaco ont defendu une designation consensuelle. Mais l'argument de l'unite ne convainc pas tous les representants africains, qui refusent de voir un scrutin ecarte pour preserver les equilibres diplomatiques souhaites par Paris. L'enjeu est egalement arithmetique et politique. Les etats africains representent 27 des 53 membres de plein droit de l'OIF. Une majorite qui donne au continent un poids determinant dans l'issue du scrutin, a condition que les delegations puissent exercer leur choix sans pression exterieure. La Republique democratique du Congo a, de son cote, officiellement apporte son soutien a Dacian Ciolos. Sa ministre des Affaires etrangeres, Therese Kayikwamba Wagner, a annonce le retrait de la candidature de Juliana Amato Lumumba et invite les autres etats a soutenir l'ancien responsable roumain. Cette position s'inscrit dans le prolongement des tensions entre Kinshasa et Kigali, le president Felix Tshisekedi ayant menace de retirer son pays de l'OIF en cas de reelection de Louise Mushikiwabo. Kagame accuse Macron de diviser la francophonie Les desaccords ont pris une dimension supplementaire le 15 novembre, lors d'un echange particulierement tendu entre Emmanuel Macron et Paul Kagame, dans les coulisses du sommet de Phnom Penh. Selon les informations de Jeune Afrique, le president rwandais a directement reproche a son homologue francais de constituer « le facteur de division unique » du sommet, en raison de ses « propres agendas » et de ses « propres interets ». Il aurait egalement denonce l'attitude de Paris et sa volonte d'imposer ses vues aux autres membres de l'organisation. Malgre les tentatives d'explication du president francais, la discussion aurait donne lieu a des eclats de voix. a son issue, Kigali a maintenu sa position : Louise Mushikiwabo restera candidate jusqu'au terme du processus. Parallelement, la delegation francaise poursuivait ses demarches aupres des representants africains pour tenter de reunir les soutiens necessaires a une solution negociee. Lors de l'ouverture officielle du sommet, ce 15 novembre, Emmanuel Macron a de nouveau plaide pour le consensus, estimant que l'elargissement de l'OIF imposait de preserver son unite. Une position a laquelle Louise Mushikiwabo a oppose une distinction : « L'unite de l'OIF ne suppose pas l'uniformite des positions. »

items.title: Abu Trica jury trial scheduled for Feb 8, 2027; Court sets Dec 15 deadline if he wants a plea deal same as Hushpuppi
items.description: Frederick Kumi, commonly known as Abu Trica, remains in US federal custody with a new jury trial date scheduled for February 8, 2027. This is following a pre-trial hearing on November 3, 2026, during which the court granted the defence and prosecution additional time to review extensive evidence in the complex fraud case. At the November 3, 2026, pre-trial hearing, the court established several key deadlines leading up to the trial. Abu Trica has a December 15, 2026, deadline to finalise any potential plea deal agreement. This means if Abu Trica decides to do a plea deal, same as what Hushpuppi did in a similar case, both sides, the defence and the prosecution have until December 15, 2026 to inform the court. The court will hold a final pre-trial conference on January 13, 2027, at 11a.m. The trial is set to begin on February 8, 2027 at 9am. Read also: ‘I am not guilty’ – Abu Trica denies charges as US court sets September 8 for trial Case overview and charges The prosecutors in the Northern District of Ohio in the United States indicted Abu Trica on charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, which carry a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. According to the US Department of Justice, Abu Trica and his co-conspirators allegedly used online dating platforms and AI-driven video tools to assume fake identities. They are accused of defrauding more than 80 elderly US citizens out of over $8 million between April 2023 and November 2025. He was arrested in Ghana in December 2025 in a joint operation involving the Ghana Cyber Security Authority. He was formally extradited to the United States on July 9, 2026. Related conviction In a connected crackdown, Ghanaian twin brothers Jamal and Kamal Abubakari and US citizen Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie pleaded guilty in October 2026 to running a separate $9 million international romance scam network. Since new court filings and trial updates are expected ahead of the December plea deadline and February trial, if Abu Trica takes a plea deal, he could get a lesser sentence than the 20 years. In the similar Ramon Abbas, widely known as Ray HushpuppiHushpuppi case for instance, where he did a plea deal, he was sentenced to 135 months (over 11 years) in a U.S. federal prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy to engage in money laundering and cyber-enabled fraud.
